title: Passivated alloy and bare iron are not equivalent aqueous inputs
original_forecast: The declared passive-film accessibility rule can distinguish the alloy material from bare iron. The result must not be generalized to immunity of all stainless steels in every chloride environment.
original_limitations: Alloy grade, pitting potential, crevice geometry and breakdown of the passive film are outside this simplified barrier rule.
lock_qualification: Producer-reported manifest hash; artifact omits raw Cargo.lock bytes.

assessment.model_scope: Matched Fe/water/salt/air/O2 and clocks isolate a declared provenance-owned accessibility barrier from bare-iron oxidation. Independent4Fe:3O2:2Fe2O3 state changes agree with actual extent; unresolved coating/alloy remains, air and retained gas are fully counted. This is the original bounded barrier question, not computed chromium passivation, coating defects, pitting immunity, surface-area matching or calibrated corrosion rate.

equal_electrolyte_conductivity.note: past I = 0.10 mol/kgw a sum of limiting molar conductivities is no longer a calibrated reading: the ion–ion drag is corrected by an empirical factor (0.86× the infinite-dilution sum here), fitted to sodium and potassium chloride between 0.01 and 2 mol/kgw. Charge type and ion size are not in the correction, so a 2:2 salt is a weaker claim than a 1:1 one

reason.en: this iron came in as stainless steel, and stainless steel does not rust for a reason ordinary steel cannot borrow: its chromium reacts with oxygen faster than the iron does and builds a chromium(III) oxide film a couple of nanometres thick, transparent, tightly bound, and self-repairing — scratch it and it reforms out of the same air that would have rusted the iron. Iron oxide is none of those things: it is loose, it flakes, and it exposes fresh metal underneath, which is why rust does not stop and a passive film does

reason.en: nothing rusts in this vessel, because there is no oxygen in it. Corrosion needs three things at once — the metal, liquid water and oxygen — since it is a circuit: {name} would give up electrons at the anode, oxygen would take them at the cathode, and the water carries the ions between the two. This bench does not yet draw oxygen from the room into an open beaker, so the oxygen has to be put in the vessel for the slow clock to see it{and_then}
